articles.fullText:
Secretary for Culture, Sports & Tourism Rosanna Law today congratulated Hong Kong athletes on winning three silver and three bronze medals at the 5th Asian Para Games across swimming, table tennis and fencing.

Swimmer Chan Yui-lam bagged a silver medal in the Women's 200m Individual Medley SM14 event, following her previous success in the butterfly, backstroke, and relay events. Miss Law noted that the results demonstrated Chan Yui-lam’s all-around prowess.

The table tennis team also achieved another milestone, collectively winning two silver and two bronze medals in the doubles events. Chiu Kan-shan and Wong Yue-ching claimed a silver medal in the Women's Doubles - Class WD14 event, while Ng Mui-wui and Wong Ting-ting bagged a silver medal in Women's Doubles - Class WD22 event.

In addition, Ho Ka-sing and Wong Chi-yin earned a bronze medal in the Men's Doubles - Class MD18 event, while Wan Wai-lok and Yuen King-shing claimed a bronze medal in the Men's Doubles - Class MD22 event.

Miss Law said it was a truly gratifying achievement, noting that the table tennis team has now amassed a total of 15 medals – five silver and 10 bronze – in the Asian Para Games.

The sports chief also congratulated fencer Yu Chui-yee on winning a bronze medal in the Women's Sabre Category A event with an outstanding performance.

Tomorrow marks the final day of the Games. Miss Law urged the public to cheer on Hong Kong’s fencing and boccia athletes.

articles.title: Stocks retreat as tech mood sours, oil prices jump
articles.excerpt: Equities sank Thursday as tech firms resumed their downward spiral after a mixed bag of earnings from Wall Street titans…
articles.fullText:
Equities sank Thursday as tech firms resumed their downward spiral after a mixed bag of earnings from Wall Street titans, while rising oil prices soured sentiment.

AI-linked companies continued the rollercoaster ride they have endured since hitting record highs in June amid worries over colossal investment sums and their timeline for profitability, with growing debt-servicing costs adding to the uncertainty.

A blockbuster quarterly report from Elon Musk's SpaceX, its first since listing in June, provided what some hoped would be solid support heading into a crucial earnings season, helping push all three main Wall Street indexes higher Wednesday.

But mixed after-hours releases from Meta and Tesla muddied the waters again for investors.

Tesla announced lower profits in July-September and cut its capital spending forecast for this year, while Facebook-parent Meta lifted its estimates for how much it would spend on artificial intelligence.

Shares of Tesla shed 1.3 percent at the start of trading in New York, while those of Meta slumped 6.7 percent.

"Risk-off sentiment is returning amid high geopolitical tensions and a swirl of worries about financing the AI juggernaut," noted Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.

Wall Street's main indices moved lower, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropping 1.3 percent.

The reports come as traders speculate about the AI boom's outlook, with analysts noting that markets fret when firms ramp up spending but also grow concerned when they pull back.

"Meta's numbers reinforce the AI investment cycle, but funding is becoming an increasingly important part of the conversation," said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone.

"Investors will reward growth and monetisation, yet they're also becoming more sensitive to how the next leg of investment is financed and what it means for existing shareholders," he added.

Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet are due to report next week, with Apple and Nvidia up in November.

European stock markets, which feature far fewer major tech firms, were lower in afternoon deals.

The Paris CAC 40 shed 1.0 percent amid concerns over France's high government debt and recent violent street protests across the country.

Barclays dipped 0.5 percent in London after revealing it would cut about 5,000 jobs by year-end as AI increasingly replaces support roles. (AFP)

Edited by Raymond Yeung

articles.title: The Download: computing’s next leap and permafrost’s climate threat
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

How far can we push computing?

On a December evening in 1959, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom.” There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued. We simply had not built the tools yet.

He was right, and for decades, computing took us into that space almost for free, as transistors repeatedly halved in size. But that easy descent has now stalled. Today, the industry is increasingly turning to brute force, building ever-bigger data centers to boost performance.

Yet the laws of physics leave plenty of room for improvement.

Here’s how researchers are exploring ways to unlock the next leap in computing .

—Volkan Gurses

This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine: The Impossible issue . Subscribe now to read it in full .

It’s also part of MIT Technology Review Explains , our series exploring the ideas shaping technology. Read more from the series .

Three things you should know about permafrost

How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.

The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just helicoptered into Alaska’s forests to report on the fires threatening permafrost and their complicated potential climate effects .

Here are three things I took away from his reporting .

—Casey Crownhart

This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

Roundtables: a conversation with the creator of AI-designed viruses

Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King offered a preliminary answer by using a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next.

In our latest Roundtables conversation, MIT Technology Review senior AI reporter James O’Donnell spoke with King about his work, being named one of our Innovators Under 35 , and new ways of seeing biology. Subscribers can now watch a full recording of the event .

Want to join the next conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 AI has uncovered a decade-old flaw threatening much of the web
It found flaws in PHP, the code behind most websites. ( Reuters $)
+ Governments are urging website owners to patch PHP or take sites offline. ( BBC )
+ Exploit attempts jumped from thousands to millions after disclosure. ( Axios )
+ Now is a good time for doing crime. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 Hackers used Claude and Grok to automate attacks on over 400 banks
The AI agents targeted financial institutions in Latin America. ( Information $)
+ Unvetted AI agents are also accessing US bank accounts. ( Axios )
+ Barclays says AI is allowing the bank to cut 5,000 jobs. ( Guardian )
+ AI is making online crimes easier. ( MIT Technology Review )

3 The Pentagon has cleared the DHS to test a heat ray weapon
It could be used for crowd control at the southern US border. ( CNN )
+ It uses invisible energy beams to produce a burning sensation. ( Axios )

4 A startup says AI-designed viruses have treated their first patient
The experimental treatment targets drug-resistant E. coli. ( NYT $)
+ But the company has not published peer-reviewed results. ( Futurism )
+ AI-designed viruses are already killing bacteria. ( MIT Technology Review )

5 Japan hopes to return the first samples from Mars’s moons
Its spacecraft is now on its way to Phobos. ( Guardian )
+ It aims to reveal whether Mars was once habitable. ( Economist $)

6 Meta faces a $25 billion penalty over the Cambridge Analytica scandal
The company says it will appeal the New Mexico ruling. ( CNBC )
+ A Meta share deal has convinced Mark Zuckerberg to stay in California. ( WSJ $)
+ Until the company remade its stock structure to help him pay it. ( NYT $)

7 A new antimatter experiment could open the door to new physics
Scientists hope to spot differences between matter and antimatter. ( Nature )

8 China’s Unitree is pitching its latest humanoid as a robot bodyguard
A promotional clip shows the H2-X disarming attackers. ( SCMP )

9 Just Eat has apologised for bizarre AI-generated menu pictures
Users were unimpressed by the bacon in cola and cheese sushi. ( BBC )

10 Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do chores
Hosts are threatening to strike, but guests are celebrating. ( Wired $)

Quote of the day

“Now they’ve given everybody a reason not to use Starlink: that Starlink isn’t reliable for national security for anybody but Trump. Maybe he’d turn it off on the United States if he didn’t like policy and he didn’t like the president.”

—SpaceX investor Ross Gerber tells CNN that Elon Musk’s decision to restrict Ukraine’s Starlink access has made the service a liability for every other government that relies on it.

One more thing

Online harassment is entering its AI era

Scott Shambaugh didn’t think twice when he denied an AI agent’s request to contribute to matplotlib, a software library he helps manage. Then things got weird.

In the middle of the night, Shambaugh opened his email to discover the agent had retaliated with a blog post. Titled “Gatekeeping in Open Source: The Scott Shambaugh Story,” the post accused him of rejecting the code out of a fear of being supplanted by AI. “He tried to protect his little fiefdom,” the agent wrote. “It’s insecurity, plain and simple.”

Shambaugh isn’t alone in facing misbehaving agents—and they’re unlikely to stop at harassment. Read the full story .

—Grace Huckins

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ These tiny experiments could work better than big life goals.
+ You can now fly around the world in Google Earth’s browser-based flight simulator .
+ A blind dressage horse is winning competitions after adopting an extraordinary form of equine “braille.”
+ Leave a book, take a book, and discover reading spots nearby in this online community of over 37,000 neighborhood libraries ,

articles.title: Evergrande liquidators recover US$435m in asset sales
articles.excerpt: China Evergrande Group's liquidators have recovered US$435.9 million from asset sales and loan recoveries so far, highlighting the challenge of…
articles.fullText:
China Evergrande Group's liquidators have recovered US$435.9 million from asset sales and loan recoveries so far, highlighting the challenge of repaying creditors with claims of about US$46 billion against the developer.

In their second progress report since a Hong Kong court ordered Evergrande's liquidation in January 2024, the liquidators, Edward Middleton and Tiffany Wong of Alvarez & Marsal, said on Thursday they aimed to make a first interim dividend payment to creditors in the first half of 2027, although the amount has yet to be determined.

Evergrande, once China's top property developer, defaulted on most of its roughly US$300 billion in liabilities.

The liquidators said they had raised the US$435.9 million through the sale of assets including aircraft, artwork and club memberships, as well as the settlement of loan receivables.

They said 96 of the 107 artworks found at Evergrande's Hong Kong headquarters had been sold for US$28.8 million at a loss. The collection included works by Picasso, Monet and Warhol, as well as sculptures by Moore and Hepworth.

Other assets being sold include a private jet expected to fetch about US$12 million in the fourth quarter. The liquidators are also seeking a US$2 million refund from a US university for part of a donation made in 2020. (Reuters)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Making the case for context-aware AI
articles.excerpt: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a…
articles.fullText:
Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes.

For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know.

The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling.

This approach could also change how employees spend their time. Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions. Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents.

Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales. With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly. As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.”

This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis.

Full Transcript

Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.

This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis.

Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads. After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized.

Two words for you: context matters.

My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis.

Welcome, Devavrat.

Devavrat Shah: Hello, Megan. Thanks for having me here.

Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today. Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale?

Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question. And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned. As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises.

The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization. We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes. There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency. In either of them, we have some processes in place. You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first. Many of us help coordinate those things. Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task. And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision.

Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate. And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context. You can’t just do that in a vacuum. And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise. And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come.

Megan: Right. To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making. If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play?

Devavrat: Fantastic. Let’s just take the setting I was describing. We are trying to automate a role or support a role or augment a role depending on the type of decision, depending upon type of task. And let’s for a second imagine that all these, as they’re called, frontier labs have built these amazing models and amazing AI infrastructure so that everything that’s happened in the universe and it’s likely to happen in the universe is all there.

Now, we have a small decision that we want to make for that very specific context is there. And without having access to that, this massive system, this extremely bright person would figure that out eventually by asking lots of questions, the way we do it as humans, and then finally do the right thing. The problem is to get to that, it will do so much compute at some level that to get simple tasks done, we are spending massive amount of compute. So that’s scenario one.

In reality, that’s not going to be the scenario, and we’ll miss some important context, important constraint, important guardrail, and then we’ll make a mistake. And sometimes that mistake can be okay. It’s like me giving you a recommendation saying, go restaurant A, and maybe you may not enjoy the dinner, versus sometimes mistakes will be very, very expensive. That is me telling you what the financial forecast is and somehow that leads to the company’s doom.

Megan: Right. So in an enterprise setting, these are really business critical decisions that are being made. So the impact is that much more if we get this wrong, isn’t it? And on a practical level then, what are the different ways that organizations can add in this context layer we’re talking about? How does Celonis, for example, deliver that operational context via a real time digital twin of an organization?

Devavrat: Absolutely. I think if it might be useful just to double click on the history of Celonis. As you know, Celonis, as an organization, came into existence with the mission, with the goal of helping organizations adhere to their ideal processes, build better processes, enable people to work with multiple processes in an intertwined manner. And that’s where their primary, let’s call it a DNA, has been about what I would call process intelligence. Take how enterprises help put multiple things together, digitize them, enable people to get their processes better, understand where the issues are, and then how do you re-engineer the process within organizations so that things can happen better.

Now, if you want to bring decision intelligence into this, each atomic step of this process that was potentially was done before by experts, people, now we want agents to help us enable that. And that’s where knowing this context of a process within enterprise and then bringing AI agents along with that, what I would like to call it as a roled agents, exactly provide the right way to bring decision intelligence to enterprises. And this is how Celonis brings context to help enterprise make better decision.

Megan: Right. And then in terms of how this works as well, how does the context layer relate to both the layer below, that’s the systems of record layer, and also the layer above, that identic layer?

Devavrat: That’s a fantastic question, Megan. The layer below primarily is, if we call it system of record, primarily it’s the workflow tools that are there and then the event logs that they generate around it. The layer above is either business user experts consuming information, or they’re consuming that information maybe through agents working on top of that context layer. And this is where the way context model, as Celonis calls it, is designed is to do three things simultaneously. One is to get the right abstraction of the layer below, so that the right pieces of the process can be agentified. Two is to bring the rolled agents for each of these pieces in a structured guardrailed manner. And then the three is to be agent first so that if there are other agentic infrastructure that are already talking to it, they can naturally talk to it so that then they can bring the right output for humans or experts to review, look at it, approve, and maybe then at times automate.

Megan: Fantastic. And for all the benefits that we’re talking about with this, are there also challenges when it comes to implementing a context layer? For example, do most organizations have the right data in place to provide AI with the context it needs? And if not, I wonder what some of the practical steps are that they might need to take to address that.

Devavrat: It’s again, a crucial question to make this real. We can imagine an ideal world, but if we cannot reach the ideal world, then it’s just ideal. So now in this setting, as we discussed the three layers, one being the layer which is the layer below system of record and workflow tools. In some sense, those things already exist. They don’t need to be complete. They don’t need to be in the cleanest possible manner. The way context model is designed with agentic’s architecture, it manages to connect to those things and make sense of it.

And then things on top is very much in control of Celonis’s infrastructure, so it’s not that complicated. The crucial thing here though is when one goes to enterprise, when one opens up, let’s say a system of record or workflow tool, event logs or things like that, one has to go through, what I would call, classical InfoSec to make sure that you can trust a vendor’s software that’s coming into your organization. And I think that is the primary process that is a step between, before and after, if I may call it.

Megan: Right. So that’s the real crucial step for people to be taking here. And as AI agents with context are able to make more complex, more accurate hopefully decisions, I wonder what you think the role of human intelligence and input will be moving forward, and how can organizations perhaps strike the balance between the two?

Devavrat: There are the benefits and then there are the challenges. Benefits are clear. If you have right AI agents in a right role manner going through your decision processes, hopefully they’re doing it quicker and hence your decisions are taken earlier so that your opportunity cost is not lost. You are taking decisions in time, you can plan much better, et cetera, et cetera. This is especially useful when you have to take very manual, repetitive, grungy tasks where access to workforce, coordination between people become crucial parts of the decision process. In a sense, that’s where the huge value can come in. The flip side of that is that means that people won’t be doing that.

On the other hand, the other type of decision that we always make, which are strategic decisions. It could be a small strategic decision, it could be large strategic decision, but the strategic decisions that typically most organizations don’t have bandwidth to take to think, that opportunity would open up and that’s where likely lots of humans and experts would engage more. In a sense, now they would have better support helping them rationally think through what are the choices that they have, how do different choices compare? And then at the end of the day, it’s organization’s role to decide which of the option to take because it belongs to their interest in mind where they want to go.

And so in a sense, there will be what I would call shift of workforce in terms of instead of doing a lot more repetitive, a lot less repetitive, but a lot more strategic work and that’s where people will have to spend time.

The other place where I am personally very optimistic is like every technology change creates new work that it’s difficult to predict at the time of change. My hope is that there will be another type of opportunity and work that will be created where we’ll be engaging our workforce. Goes without saying, this would mean that we will have to carefully think through reeducating or educating some of our workforce thoughtfully. And I think as an academic in me, as an educator in me, I really feel that the timescale at which these changes are happening are so fast. So we need to also act in a similar manner.

Megan: For any decision maker listening to this, how should they start implementing these changes? For example, how can they prepare their workforce? What role should governance play as well?

Devavrat: Okay, that’s a great question. If you want to start, the first thing you need to do is identify a decision where you want to bring intelligence. Let’s identify the process around it. Let’s identify each step of the process. Let’s take the most crucial, difficult step in that. Let’s try to bring AI agents to help you to do that. And then from there you go and then let’s measure how much speed are we getting, how much value are we getting? And that’ll help us understand whether this was worth it. So that’s one.

Second is governance. Well, we’re going to bring AI in this prescriptive manner for each task in a role. That means that for that role, we can tell what it can or cannot do very clearly. And Celonis prescribes certified role agents for these things. This helps you clearly have an understanding of what sort of contract would be for this.

And the third thing, which is people, and now this is where it’s really important, is a part which gets automated, but then there’s a part where experts will be in the loop and this is where they need to understand the outputs of AI, how do you work with that and what its implication would be? And this is where some AI education is needed and then some tool education is needed.

Megan: Yes, absolutely. The pace is incredible, isn’t it, in this space? And speaking of, I suppose if we could close with a look ahead, given the right context, of course, what are the use cases perhaps for enterprise AI that are on the horizon that you think could be most impactful or perhaps what you’re simply most excited about?

Devavrat: I think I would categorize them into three types. They’re all decision intelligence, decision-making, but there are three types. One, what I would call many repetitive manual labor-intensive, so that’s one.

Two, what I would call coordination style tasks. A lot of work that we do right now as an information workforce that’s spent in coordination, that’s why email spreadsheets, et cetera. A lot of that would be done much better, much quicker and less boring, so to speak.

And then the third is where, especially as a support to human decision-makers to provide strategic support augmentation, and that’s a third type of decisions that would be done. If I think of any planning process in enterprises, so financial planning, workforce planning, marketing, sales, product, anything, all of those are business critical decisions that we make that take annual planning process, take annual time. Now maybe it should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.

Megan: That’d be fantastic, wouldn’t it? Fantastic. Thank you so much for that brilliant conversation, Devavrat. That was Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England.

That’s it for this episode of Business Lab. I’m your host, Megan Tatum. I’m a contributing editor and host for Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. We were founded in 1899 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and you can find us in print, on the web, and at events each year around the world. For more information about us and the show, please check out our website at technologyreview.com.

This show is available wherever you get your podcasts. And if you enjoyed this episode, we hope you’ll take a moment to rate and review us. Business Lab is a production of MIT Technology Review, and this episode was produced by Giro Studios. Thanks so much for listening. Goodbye.

articles.title: Three things you should know about permafrost
articles.excerpt: How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is…
articles.fullText:
How much do you know about permafrost?

Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.

The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just published two in-depth stories about permafrost. His reporting took him to the boreal forests of Alaska, where he helicoptered into the wilderness to learn more about how this material could affect our climate both now and in the future.

I’d recommend you give both of James’s stories a read. There’s this feature about efforts to tackle the intensifying fires that are threatening permafrost, as well as this look at how researchers are trying to understand the complicated tangle of potential climate effects. Here are three things I took away.

Permafrost is a massive blind spot for climate change

Permafrost is the frozen layer of soil that’s under about 15% of land around the Northern Hemisphere. While technically material needs to be frozen for only two consecutive years to count as permafrost, most of our current permafrost formed during the last ice age.

That means there’s organic material that’s been frozen, and essentially locked away, for thousands of years. But as global temperatures tick up and this layer thaws, microbes are able to break down that organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane—powerful greenhouse gases that drive climate change. Those emissions form a feedback loop, accelerating warming further.

The steady rise in global temperatures has already shrunk the footprint of the Arctic permafrost by about 12% since 1850, and the pace has been picking up in the last 50 years.

The wild thing is, only a minority of the models that have been used in UN climate reports actually take into account the gradual loss of permafrost. And none of them include the abrupt thaw and collapse that can happen after events like heat waves and fires (more on those fires in a moment). There are efforts to make sure future UN reports reflect the growing science, but for now, all this means that we’re probably underestimating how much and how fast the planet is going to warm.

Wildfires can speed up permafrost loss

Fire is a natural part of boreal forests’ life cycle, but they’re getting more intense because of climate change. And crucially, fires can accelerate the thawing of permafrost. By the end of the century, this effect could release the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide.

Today, the policy across remote parts of Canada and Alaska is generally to let wildfires burn as long as they’re not threatening human habitats. But some researchers say we should explore fighting these fires to save the carbon trapped in the forests and the permafrost beneath them.

Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center are developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across Alaska, essentially highlighting areas where fires are most likely to spread and which areas are home to certain types of permafrost that would release the most emissions. (Yes, apparently there are different types of permafrost. Yedoma is a particularly deep, carbon-dense form from the late Pleistocene era.)

That’s all just the beginning—once we figure out potential targets, the question is what to do about it. Some suggest setting more prescribed fires, something Indigenous groups have done for thousands of years, partly to reduce the danger of massive blazes. Or resources could go to early detection and efforts to put out fires before they grow.

The carbon cycle of permafrost is incredibly complicated

There’s about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon locked away in permafrost, about twice the amount in the atmosphere. We know that permafrost thawing can release greenhouse-gas emissions and drive climate change. But there are complications.

One particularly big wrinkle: Other effects from permafrost thawing and fire recovery might counteract the carbon lost from those events. For example, as temperatures warm, plants can gradually move north and take hold where they couldn’t have before. Those plants soak up carbon from the atmosphere as they grow, at least partly locking away what was emitted.

Researchers are working to better understand this ecosystem. And the more we learn, the more complicated the picture looks. How much carbon is lost from permafrost, and how much a given area will recover its carbon, depend on a huge array of factors. How severe are the fires that have accelerated local thawing? What’s the local climate and environment? And what kind of permafrost is at stake?

The higher we push the planet’s temperature, the more we mess with complicated natural phenomena that we’re only beginning to understand.

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

articles.title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
articles.excerpt: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and…
articles.fullText:
Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs.

What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning.

As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it

Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind.

Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. That’s a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw. Scale this to an enterprise generating longer, higher resolution video and the back-end footprint grows into the hundreds of gigabytes per clip.

And that back-end footprint is growing fast. McKinsey projects AI inference demand will grow at a 35% CAGR through 2030, versus 22% for training, making up more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade.

A recent WD-sponsored IDC global white paper that surveyed 763 IT and business decision makers found that nearly 95% of respondents reported an increase in data volume due to generative AI over the past 12 months, with roughly 61% reporting growth of 25% or more.

“You can think of having more storage as an optimization for keeping the GPUs busy,” said a senior product manager of a hyperscale cloud service provider quoted in report. “The biggest challenge is to ensure that the GPUs are not idle, waiting for data to show up—hours of GPU idle time becomes very expensive, very fast.” Put in dollar terms: if your storage spend is growing 25% year over year while your compute budget grows in the more predictable cyclical way, storage ends up outpacing the budget line that receives the most attention.

Matching storage to the AI data life cycle

Compute demand rises and falls with training cycles, product launches, and hardware refreshes. But the volume of retained data doesn’t fall back down with it when compute demand slows. Model logs, synthetic outputs, inference results, and more keep accumulating, and organizations are holding onto more of it for longer.

This changes the role of retained data. Information that once moved into an archive and rarely surfaced can now become an input to future AI workloads. As more data is retained, retrieved, and reused, storage must support not only growing capacity, but increasingly dynamic access to it. The same WD-IDC survey found 96% of respondents anticipate needing faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

AI workloads require both performance and capacity, with different technologies serving different needs across the data lifecycle. And for the vast volumes of data that must be retained and revisited, HDDs provide a cost-effective, high-capacity foundation, with a significant cost-per-terabyte advantage

What this means for how AI gets budgeted

For a CFO or CIO, this means “AI infrastructure spend” may be scoped too narrowly on compute. A model that idles while data loads costs about as much as one idling for lack of a GPU. But the storage bottleneck stays hidden until it’s already a problem, surfacing in operating costs and retrieval delays rather than a CapEx line next to the accelerators.

Consider a retailer generating AI product videos for its catalog, or an insurer running claims documents through a RAG pipeline for faster underwriting. In both cases, the compute cost is a known, budgeted quantity: a per-generation or per-query rate that finance can forecast. The storage cost is different: It compounds with every video generated and every claim processed, because none of that back-end data disappears once the task is finished.

A team that budgets AI as “compute plus a rounding error for storage” may find, in 12 to 18 months, that the rounding error has become a significant fraction of the program’s total cost—right around the time leadership is deciding whether to expand.

Building for economically scalable capacity

Addressing this challenge starts with architecture. Storage strategy tends to be designed for expensive, hot-tier performance (for data accessed instantly and constantly), while most AI data by volume accumulates in the warm, cool, and cold tiers behind it.

What enterprises need is economically scalable capacity: Infrastructure designed for the full AI data life cycle, balancing performance with capacity, power, reliability, and total cost of ownership as data persists, compounds, and is increasingly reused. That means treating archives that once sat untouched as active assets for RAG and inference, and setting retention policies for data’s growing strategic value rather than its original storage cost. It also means recognizing that decisions about storage play out across fleets, not individual drives.

Such infrastructure requires storage tiers, where individualized power consumption, reliability, density, and operational efficiency all determine whether the system remains economically sustainable as capacity scales.

There are three questions to ask about your organization’s AI infrastructure budget:

- What’s our data retention policy for AI-generated content, and who set(s) it?

- Is our storage procurement tied to training-time performance needs, or to the actual life cycle of the data we’re producing?

- If our AI usage doubled next year, would our storage cost double with it, or worse?

Most organizations cannot answer all three with confidence. That’s the gap worth closing before the next budget cycle, not after.

articles.title: 'China, Russia are valuable force for stability'
articles.excerpt: Premier Li Qiang said on Wednesday said China and Russia have served as a valuable force for stability in a…
articles.fullText:
Premier Li Qiang said on Wednesday said China and Russia have served as a valuable force for stability in a world marked by turbulence and transformation, as he said Beijing stands ready to enhance cooperation with Moscow.

Li was speaking during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg.

Xinhua news agency quoted Li as saying that China is ready to work with Russia to deepen practical cooperation in areas such as energy resources, trade and investment, and transportation, and achieve more positive outcomes.

Beijing is also ready to strengthen communication and coordination with Moscow on major issues, and maintain close cooperation within multilateral platforms such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and Brics, Li added. He said both sides should unite more forces of the Global South to safeguard common interests and uphold fairness and justice.

For his part, Putin said relations between the neighbours are built on the basis of equality and mutual respect, while noting that bilateral relations are not affected by changes in the international landscape and not subject to interference from any third party.

China has been and will always be Russia's closest and most reliable partner, Putin said.

Russia is ready to deepen practical cooperation with China in areas such as energy, agriculture, space, civilian nuclear energy, information technology, artificial intelligence and transportation, he added. (Reporting by Xinhua)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Duterte impeachment: bribing elites is China’s strategy, military official says
articles.excerpt: Philippine government launches national security probes into Chinese influence.
articles.fullText:
MANILA - If Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte accepted funds from Beijing to grant political favors, it would fall directly within standard operating procedures for Chinese foreign influence operations, a Philippine military official told Radio Free Asia.
The remarks came after prosecutors in the vice president’s impeachment trial presented evidence of the alleged corruption – a financial forensics accountant testified that Cale88 Foods Corp., controlled by Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio, received 319 million pesos (US$5 million) from state-run Chinese firms. Duterte said the allegations were politically motivated.
The revelations raised alarm bells, with Filipino officials and experts immediately raising the specter of Chinese spy and malign influence operations as the two countries have become locked in an increasingly tense territorial dispute in the South China Sea, parts of which are claimed by Manila and referred to as the West Philippine Sea.
The competing claims in the South China Sea.
(RFA) Gaining access to the most influential people in a target country is a fundamental malign influence strategy for Beijing, retired Rear Adm. Roy Vincent Trinidad, spokesman for the Philippine military in the West Philippine Sea, told RFA.
“Part of the rulebook of the Chinese Communist Party includes economic elite co-optation and political elite co-optation,” Trinidad told RFA. “If they could co-opt a political leader, have him elected by building him up politically through foreign malign influence, they would have achieved the objective without firing a single shot.”
While donations or grants by any government are not illegal per se and are governed by rules, if the supposed investments are “used to advance the position of our adversary…it will have very serious national security implications,” Trinidad said.
“When another country would like to occupy your territory, would like to sow false narratives to advance their interests, they are creating trouble not only domestically, but in the region,” he stressed.
Going bananas?
Duterte was impeached in May for large-scale corruption and death threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., her former political ally turned nemesis.
The prosecution on Oct. 13 dropped three of the charges – misuse of funds, bribery, and grave threats – to speed up the trial, but she still remains accused of having unexplained wealth.
During the trial proceedings earlier in the month, the Anti-Money Laundering Council said the funds paid to the food company controlled by Duterte and her husband were in suspiciously high amounts for what they had been reported as – payment for banana chips, and that the firm did not have the operational capabilities that matched those payments.
Banana chips are displayed at a food show in Paris, Oct. 20, 2014.
(Bertrand Guay/AFP) The defense cited customs records that showed outgoing banana chip shipments with a declared value of 217 million pesos ($3.4 million), which is still about 100 million pesos less than the payments received.
Additionally, the trial revealed that the company had only two employees, which Senator-Judge Joel Villanueva during the proceedings said was “alarming” considering the company’s reported revenue and sales.
Government officials cannot be the direct beneficiary of funds from any foreign government, Leila de Lima, one of the prosecutors in Duterte’s impeachment trial, told RFA. She called the case a “substantiation of financial infusion by China” to influence.
“VP Sara’s receipt of funds from China without any exempting justification such as a legitimate business squarely constitutes a betrayal of her oath and disloyalty to the Philippines,” she said. “There can only be one reason for the receipt of hundreds of millions of pesos in monetary benefits by a public official from a foreign government.”
China’s Embassy in Manila did not immediately respond when contacted by RFA. But in a short statement it issued on Oct. 5, the embassy urged “relevant individuals in the Philippines to stop political manipulation and not drag Philippine domestic politics into China-Philippine relations.”
“A serious matter”
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., talking to reporters during a visit to Singapore on Oct. 11, acknowledged that the prosecution’s allegations were a “serious matter” that needed to be investigated.
If found to be true “it would go straight to the top of our list of threats that are facing the Philippines,” Marcos said, according to official transcripts of his interview with the traveling Filipino press.
“We are talking about the sovereignty of the Republic,” he said. “We are talking about the safety and security of the state. And I cannot think of any discussion that occurs at a higher level than that.”
Following Marcos’ statement, the National Security Council as well as state intelligence units were tasked to probe deeper into the allegations. The council said it took the allegations very seriously at a time of increased Chinese intelligence operations locally.
“The reported transactions and any credible information involving significant financial flows that may bear upon the country’s national security warrants careful, in-depth and responsible assessment,” national security adviser Eduardo Oban told reporters. He said the NSC will work with other agencies to assess “national security implications, if any, arising from the reported transactions.”
Alleged Chinese spy operations have been documented in the Philippines, and defense and national security officials are working to weed out Filipinos compromised by Chinese operatives. Earlier this year, RFA interviewed one of three Filipinos recently caught spying for China , who explained he had been recruited through an online advertisement.
"Danny," a Filipino who spied for China, talks to RFA at an undisclosed location in Manila, Philippines in April 2026.
(Jason Gutierrez/RFA) The military is in the process of weeding out more alleged spies through an “insider threat program” launched in 2023 and designed to protect sensitive government information, including data linked to the South China Sea.
After Marcos’ remarks, Vice President Duterte dismissed the allegations against her as political theatrics meant to target and harass her family through surveillance. “And this could have serious implications to our relationship with China,” she said.
Duterte is the daughter of former President Rodrigo Duterte, whose six-year term ended in 2022. During his presidency, the elder Duterte pursued a conciliatory stance toward Beijing—a sharp contrast to Marcos, who has leaned heavily into a U.S.-aligned foreign policy.
The younger Duterte joined forces with Marcos – himself the son of a former president – during the 2022 campaign to form an unbeatable UniTeam ticket that united the country’s two most powerful political dynasties.
The alliance between two of the leading political families in the country however soon crumbled, with Marcos in 2025 allowing the International Criminal Court to arrest Rodrigo Duterte for deaths related to his war on drugs.
Officials told RFA they would continue their operations against foreign operatives known to operate in the country. On Oct. 12, the military said its intelligence operatives helped immigration officials in raiding a hub for online gaming operations near military headquarters, and arrested 76 individuals, mostly Chinese nationals.
Operatives told RFA that the raid was part of its program to disrupt Chinese spying and malign influence operations, but declined to elaborate citing the sensitivity of the ongoing investigation.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: 'China ready for deeper cooperation with Russia'
articles.excerpt: Premier Li Qiang on Tuesday said China is ready to work with Russia to make sustained efforts to steer bilateral…
articles.fullText:
Premier Li Qiang on Tuesday said China is ready to work with Russia to make sustained efforts to steer bilateral cooperation in a direction that is deeper, more substantive and more resilient, as he arrived in St Petersburg for a regular meeting between Chinese and Russian heads of government.

A report by the Xinhua news agency also quoted Li as saying both sides will push the China-Russia comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination for the new era to yield new and fruitful results.

The premier said the two countries have jointly explored a way of getting along featuring non-alliance, non-confrontation and without targeting any third party, while continuously deepening cooperation in various fields.

China and Russia have set a fine example of relations between major countries featuring permanent good-neighbourly friendship, comprehensive strategic coordination and mutually beneficial cooperation, Li added.

In particular, under the strategic guidance of Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in recent years, China-Russia relations have become more mature and resilient, with the foundation of political mutual trust growing ever stronger, mutually beneficial cooperation becoming increasingly solid, and the bonds of friendship from generation to generation growing ever closer, he said.

The efforts made by both sides will bring greater benefits to the two peoples and inject valuable stability and certainty into world peace and development, he added. (Reporting by Xinhua)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: China-Laos air base could be another Southeast Asian forward outpost for Beijing
articles.excerpt: Like Ream Naval Base in Cambodia, Ban Keun could lay the groundwork for increased Chinese presence, analysts said.
articles.fullText:
A new joint military training facility in Laos could give Beijing a lasting foothold in mainland Southeast Asia even without an immediate boost to its combat power, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
Beijing and Vientiane opened a joint support and training center and an aviation academy at Ban Keun, about 50 kilometers north of the Lao capital, on Sept. 29. Beijing says the facility will train Lao air force pilots and it will be maintained by both countries.
The airfield, once complete, would be China’s second joint military outpost in Southeast Asia, after a Chinese-funded expansion of Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base opened in April of last year. The facility at Ream, despite its official designation as a dual-use facility, has seen a regular rotation of Chinese naval vessels.
The joint facility in Laos could allow China to deepen military ties, familiarize personnel with overseas operations and lay the groundwork for a larger presence, Joseph Kristanto, a research analyst at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, told RFA.
“Ultimately, I think the more important question is not simply whether Ban Keun could accommodate Chinese military aircraft, but whether Beijing intends to develop the facility into a sustained operational hub,” he said.
China’s Defense Ministry said in an announcement that the facility would be maintained by both countries and was “not directed against any third party.” It said its construction and use complied with domestic and international law and would strengthen military cooperation and support regional peace and stability.
Laos’ state news agency KPL reported that officials from both countries described the project at the opening ceremony as the product of cooperation based on mutual respect and equality. The facility would develop Lao military pilots’ practical skills, it said.
The locations of Ban Keun Airfield in Laos and Ream Naval Base in Cambodia.
(RFA) The KPL report also said both sides pledged to expand cooperation through joint training and exercises, personnel development and humanitarian assistance. Neither that report nor the Chinese announcement specified how many Chinese military personnel would work at Ban Keun, how long they would remain or the conditions governing Chinese aircraft deployments.
Satellite imagery analysis provided to RFA suggests some construction continued after the opening of the joint airfield. But its future military significance will depend on more than its physical completion, including the extent of Chinese access and the frequency and nature of activities there, Kristanto said.
China already operates military facilities on disputed features in the South China Sea. Ban Keun could extend its overseas presence inland, offering opportunities to build closer ties with the Lao military and gain experience operating from a foreign facility, he said.
The airfield’s immediate military advantages are less clear, analysts said. China has airbases in its own southern territory closer to the South China Sea, raising questions about what additional operations an inland facility in Laos would enable.
Strategic advantage for Beijing?
In satellite imagery of the airfield during its opening, eight aircraft are visible. Private satellite imagery analyst Jacob Bogle told RFA they were K-8, also known as JL-8, light attack and training aircraft.
Chinese JL-8 planes perform maneuvers in southern China's Guangdong province Sept. 28, 2021.
(Noel Celis/AFP) Examining an Oct. 7 image, he identified what he thought was one remaining aircraft, while cautioning that the image was blurry. He suggested the others had likely moved into hangars, although their locations could not be established from that observation.
Bogle also identified what appeared to be workshops and temporary construction infrastructure beside the southern end of the runway.
“So while the runway and main buildings are completed, it looks like there is still some minor work that is being finished,” he said.
The imagery does not establish who owns or operates the aircraft. Both China and Laos operate the K-8 type, according to analysts cited by Reuters.
But a Lao military officer, while downplaying concerns over increased Chinese military presence in Southeast Asia, confirmed to RFA that at least some of the fighter jets at the facility are Chinese.
“It is a pilot training airport. A group of people are envious that Laos has a flight training center, yet Laos has never complained about neighboring countries hosting U.S. air bases,” said the officer on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak on such matters.
“When Laos built Ban Keun Airport for pilot training, some people overreacted. Naturally, Chinese officials brought their own fighter jets, given that it is a joint Lao-Chinese operation,” he said.
Bogle said it was too early to determine China’s future position at Ban Keun, but that the facility warranted monitoring.
This satellite image taken Oct. 7, 2026, shows that previously visible aircraft have likely been moved into their hangars. Next to the southern end of the runway are what looks like workshops and other temporary construction infrastructure.
(RFA) Kristanto said operating combat aircraft from Laos would require substantial investment in fuel storage, maintenance facilities, munitions, air defense and other supporting infrastructure.
“At present, I see little evidence that Ban Keun offers a decisive operational advantage over China’s existing facilities,” he said.
Such limitations do not rule out a broader role in the future. Ban Keun could theoretically support intelligence gathering, surveillance, logistics or forward aircraft deployments if the necessary infrastructure and access arrangements were established, he said.
Surrounding Vietnam?
A sustained Chinese military presence in Laos could add another consideration for neighboring Vietnam, which already faces China across its northern land border and contests Beijing’s claims in the South China Sea.
China’s expansive maritime claims overlap with the exclusive economic zones of Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia. Vietnam also claims the Paracel and Spratly island groups, where competing sovereignty claims are distinct from disputes over rights to surrounding waters. China controls the Paracels, while several governments occupy features in the Spratlys.
In 2016, an international arbitral tribunal rejected China’s claims to the entire South China Sea based on its controversial nine-dash line, which surrounds the whole sea. This claim was seen to exceed what Beijing could legally claim under the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Credit: RFA
Beijing rejected the decision, and has continued to assert its claims over areas that are within the exclusive economic zones of the other claimants.
China has strengthened this position through island-building and military infrastructure, including runways, surveillance equipment and air defenses on occupied reefs. Those facilities support a wider maritime presence in waters where rival claimants seek to protect fishing grounds, energy resources and access to their outposts.
Ban Keun would introduce a different geographic consideration for Hanoi, potentially bringing Chinese military activity to its western side as well.
Bogle argued that facilities in Laos and Cambodia, together with China’s South China Sea bases, had effectively encircled Vietnam.
Kristanto was more cautious. Vietnam would have to account for the possibility of a Chinese military presence beyond its northern border and the South China Sea, he said, but Ban Keun’s inland location and China’s existing airbases limit its immediate operational value.
“For now, I would characterize Ban Keun as a potentially important strategic foothold rather than a major shift in the regional military balance.”
Ream offers a comparison
China’s involvement at Cambodia’s Ream naval base shows why a facility’s use over time can be more revealing than its designation as a joint training center, the analysts said.
China financed an expansion of Ream, on Cambodia’s southern coast, where its joint support and training center opened in April 2025. Cambodia maintains that Chinese personnel and warships are not permanently based there.
An analysis published in May 2025 by the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative documented Chinese naval vessels rotating through Ream after their initial arrival in December 2023.
Chinese navy vessels are clearly visible at Ream Naval Base, Cambodia. The Chinese navy appears to have kept a near permanent presence at the base ever since December 2023, after the "Chinese pier" was completed.
(RFA) It also found that visiting Japanese and Vietnamese vessels used a different waterfront area from the large pier occupied by Chinese ships, suggesting unequal access to some facilities. Those findings described arrangements at the time and do not establish current access rules.
Kristanto said the comparison with Ban Keun was useful in examining how China could expand its military presence through partnerships that initially fall short of large, permanent bases.
“Rather than immediately establishing large, permanent military bases, Beijing appears to be pursuing arrangements that could provide access, logistical support, and opportunities for a more sustained military presence.”
The differences remain substantial. Ream provides direct access to the sea and can support naval deployments, while Ban Keun’s military utility depends heavily on the aircraft and supporting infrastructure deployed there, he added.
For the Lao facility, subsequent construction and deployments will help establish whether the training partnership develops into a broader operational role.
“Its future significance will depend on the extent of Chinese access, the infrastructure developed, and the frequency and nature of PLA activities there,” Kristanto said.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: US agencies ordered to stop using DeepSeek AI tools
articles.excerpt: The US government has ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence tools from Chinese mainland startup DeepSeek as the…
articles.fullText:
The US government has ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence tools from Chinese mainland startup DeepSeek as the two countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector.

A notice on Monday from the Department of Homeland Security announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek – and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices.

The department can issue direction to civilian agencies, but not the military or intelligence services.

"DeepSeek's models present multiple threat vectors," said a document attached to Monday's notice.

Use of DeepSeek AI tools "may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors," the department warned.

Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government "extensive authority" to access private company infrastructure, it said.

DeepSeek, one of China's top AI labs, shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance.

The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and this month updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4.

Despite their fierce competition in the field, China and the United States in September agreed to set up a "communication channel" for AI incidents.

The topic is expected to arise again when the countries' leaders meet next month at a summit in Shenzhen. (AFP)

Edited by Altis Wong

articles.title: Trump 'open to summit with Xi and Putin'
articles.excerpt: US President Donald Trump said on Monday he is open to three-way arms-control talks with President Xi Jinping and Russian…
articles.fullText:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday he is open to three-way arms-control talks with President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin as soon as next month, raising the prospect of an unprecedented meeting.

"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "If President Xi wants to have it, I'd have it. I'm sure we'd talk about other things like trade too."

The Kremlin said earlier that the Russian, Chinese and US leaders could meet at an Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen next month, following a Wall Street Journal report that Putin wanted the three-way talks to broker a peace deal favourable to Moscow.

The three leaders have met separately but never held formal talks together.

"I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much," Trump told reporters when asked if he would attend a meeting with Putin and Xi to discuss Ukraine.

Pressed on whether he would discuss Ukraine at any Xi-Putin summit, Trump replied that he would do "whatever I can do to end the war."

But Trump defended his recent diesel deal with Putin and decision to waive new sanctions on Moscow, which has opened a huge rift with Kyiv and prompted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to warn the US leader he is on the wrong side of history.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said when asked about the Ukrainian's comments. "To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."

Moscow launched one of its broadest air assaults in months overnight, cutting power to more than half a million households and damaging energy infrastructure across Ukraine. Ten people were reported killed.

Kyiv has accused Washington of withholding vital intelligence and slowing speeds on a satellite system used to track incoming strikes.

Last week, Trump told reporters he thought a denuclearisation deal with Russia and China was possible, but that it "doesn't have to be this year." It's not clear how advanced any talks between the countries are.

Russia has the most stored nuclear warheads, followed by the United States and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

The ⁠Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty expired earlier this year. The New START treaty, signed in 2010, allowed a single extension, which Putin and former US President Joe Biden agreed to for five years. Any new extension would require an executive decision to voluntarily extend the limits of the treaty.

China's foreign ministry said last week that its "nuclear strength is by no means at the same level with that of the US and Russia" and that it would be "neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage."

Trump has already agreed to attend the Apec summit in Shenzhen next month, marking his second trip to China this year and his third visit with Xi over the same period. (Agencies)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Rare photos of Aung San Suu Kyi spark renewed calls for her release
articles.excerpt: Myanmar military releases images of jailed former leader receiving books and letters from Britain’s King Charles.
articles.fullText:
Myanmar’s military-backed government released images of deposed former leader Aung San Suu Kyi receiving items sent by King Charles III of the United Kingdom, a development that brought on renewed calls for the ousted former leader’s release.
Aung San Suu Kyi has been detained since the 2021 military coup that ousted her and the rest of the country’s democratically elected government from power. She was sentenced to 18 years for a broad range of crimes that include corruption and election fraud, though she maintains that she is innocent.
For the duration of her detention, her exact location has not been easy to ascertain.
The military government moved her to house arrest in April, but still have allowed almost no contact with the outside.
Aung San Suu Kyi received an envelope that contained diplomatic communication, and two books from King Charles – “The Land Gardeners: Soil to Table” and “Soil: The ​World at Our Feet.”
The delivery – which the military government revealed in a public statement – lasted only 10 minutes. It is the first acknowledgement of the detained former leader receiving correspondence from abroad.
Family members, Myanmar watchers and world government officials told RFA that they were pleased to know she was allowed to receive the king’s message, but they warned against allowing the military to use the delivery as propaganda.
Kim Aris, the younger son of Aung San Suu Kyi, told RFA that he took comfort that his mother was in the king’s thoughts and that he appreciated the kind gesture.
“I take comfort in knowing that my mother remains in the thoughts of His Majesty King Charles III, and I sincerely appreciate his kind gesture in sending her books. However, we must not allow the military regime to use such selective disclosures to create an illusion of normality or gain international legitimacy. A gesture of kindness should never be used to distract from the continued violation of my mother’s fundamental human rights. My mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, is an 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize laureate who remains unjustly detained on politically motivated charges, hidden from the world and denied direct contact with her family and independent medical assessment. Despite recent developments, we still have no direct communication with her or credible, independently verified information about her health and wellbeing. I hope His Majesty’s thoughtful gesture will also serve as a reminder to world leaders that my mother’s situation remains unresolved. I urge all governments engaging with Min Aung Hlaing to insist on meaningful humanitarian progress, including regular, direct family contact, independent medical access, and her immediate and unconditional release, together with all political prisoners.”
Cara Chittenden, a communications officer at the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, told RFA that Aung San Suu Kyi should not be in detention.
“The UK continues to condemn the arbitrary detention of Aung San Suu Kyi and calls for her immediate and unconditional release, alongside all those arbitrarily detained in Myanmar. We remain gravely concerned about her continued detention and wellbeing. The UK has also co-sponsored a number of Human Rights Council resolutions on Myanmar, including most recently in March 2026 . The resolution condemned human rights violations against the people of Myanmar, including the Rohingya and other ethnic minorities.”
A spokesperson from the U.S. Department of State said that Washington remained “concerned about all individuals unjustly detained” and continued “to call for their release and the military to engage in genuine dialogue with all opposition groups to end the conflict in Burma. The United States remains steadfast in our support for the people of Burma.”
Aung Myo Kyaw, a spokesperson from the Thailand-based Assistance Association for Political Prisoners, told RFA that the delivery of the books and letters was a positive development.
“However, the world does not view Aung San Suu Kyi as a ‘special prisoner,’ as the regime claims (in its statement); rather, she is recognized as a national leader. Whenever the military junta faces crises on various fronts, they tend to use Daw Aung San Suu Kyi as a hidden political card. In this instance, too, their actions are merely a gesture—a performance intended to project themselves as flexible and big-hearted.”
Kyaw Htwe, an exiled member of the Central Working Committee of Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy party, told RFA that the meeting was the military engaging in political theater.
“Engagement should be measured by political progress. When they fail to bring about such political progress, they typically resort to their usual tactic: releasing news regarding our Chairperson, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, to manipulate the situation. Rather than just sending books or letters, it is necessary to allow her to meet with her family—specifically her younger son—as well as her legal team.”
That legal team is reportedly seeking to meet her in person since May 30 prison-to-private house transfer, sources close to the legal team told RFA. The legal team’s repeated requests to meet with her are ignored by military authorities.
Myint Htwe, a government leader in a part of the country not controlled by the military, said that the junta’s move to publicize the delivery was meant to try to gain legitimacy.
“These are just the same old tactics. The fact that they chose to issue a press statement—when they could have easily handled the matter quietly—suggests a softening of their stance. I interpret this as a deliberate attempt to signal—to put on full display—that they are treating a communication from the British monarch with great seriousness, as a legitimate government would. Furthermore, I see it as an effort to project the image of being a legitimate government to the rest of the world.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Uyghur activists urge Rubio to raise rights concerns with Central Asian officials
articles.excerpt: Uzbekistan trip is a chance to reassert U.S. moral leadership by pressing the C5 to protect Uyghur communities.
articles.fullText:
Uyghur advocates have urged U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to seek commitments not to deport Uyghurs to China and to protect them from Beijing’s transnational repression during his upcoming meetings with Central Asian officials, the leader of a prominent Uyghur rights organization told Radio Free Asia.
Rubio is leading a U.S. delegation of more than 200 business representatives and will arrive in Uzbekistan on Saturday for the first leg of a six-day trip that also includes two stops in India. While in Samarkand, he will attend the C5+1 ministerial meetings – with officials from the five Central Asian countries of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio boards a plane, Oct. 8, 2026, in Lisbon.
(Mark Schiefelbein/AP) According to the Washington-based Uyghur Human Rights Project, more than 400,000 Uyghurs live in these Central Asian countries and combined they form the “vast majority” of the Uyghur diaspora outside of East Turkestan, which is the name by which Uyghurs call their homeland, currently under the control of the People’s Republic of China.
As a U.S. senator, Rubio was a champion of Uyghur issues and now as Washington’s top diplomat, he is expected to discuss the safety and rights of Uyghurs with the C5 leaders, Abdureshit Abdulhamit, vice president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress, told RFA.
Abdureshit Abdulhamit, vice president of the World Uyghur Congress.
(RFA Illustration) “We urge him to seek clear commitments that no Uyghur will be forcibly returned to China, where they could face persecution, imprisonment or torture,” said Abdureshit. “Uyghurs seeking protection should have access to fair asylum procedures.”
He also urged Rubio to address intimidation and surveillance targeting Uyghur communities, saying people should be able to preserve their culture, discuss detained relatives and communicate abroad without fear.
Communities at risk
Compared to Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, Uyghurs in Uzbekistan face more challenges to their social and cultural rights, Zumretay Erkin, another vice president of the organization, told RFA.
“Uzbekistan is also complicit in deporting Uyghurs to China at the explicit request of the Chinese government,” she said. “Uyghurs are subjected to tight surveillance and transnational repression.”
Zumretay Erkin, vice president of the World Uyghur Congress.
(RFA Illustration) Zumretay said Rubio’s diplomatic visit is a “unique opportunity to raise Uyghur human rights, even in a trade and investment context,” noting that the U.S. government was among the first to take action to address the Uyghur genocide.
Washington classified China’s treatment of Uyghurs in the Uyghur region as genocide in 2021.
Moral leadership
Rubio can show the world that the United States’ moral leadership still matters, Omer Kanat, executive director of the Washington-based Uyghur Human Rights Project, wrote in an opinion piece in The Diplomat.
Kanat cited former U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo’s public calls against returning Uyghurs to China as a precedent. He also pointed to Thailand’s February 2025 deportation of 40 Uyghurs as a warning of the consequences when diplomatic efforts fail.
Omer Kanat, executive director of the Uyghur Human Rights Project.
(RFA Illustration) “This upcoming trip to Central Asia gives Rubio a chance to show that the United States won’t countenance a repeat of that tragedy,” he wrote. “With the right messaging, the trip can fortify China’s neighbors to stand firm against Beijing’s pressure to return Uyghurs to China.”
The WUC also called on Rubio to hear directly from Uyghur representatives and establish follow-up mechanisms for individual cases.
“We would judge the visit by concrete results: stronger protection against deportation, action on cases of harassment and a clear American commitment to follow through after the meetings end,” said Abdureshit.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Tibetan rights group: South Africa arson attack is transnational repression by CCP
articles.excerpt: Police are still investigating the firebombing of the Dalai Lama representative’s home office in South Africa.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Tibetan.
Authorities are still investigating Wednesday’s firebombing of the Dalai Lama’s representative office in South Africa, police told Radio Free Asia, as activists accused China of having a hand in the attack.
'Transnational repression' by China, Tibet activists say
The office of the Tibetan spiritual leader in Pretoria suffered extensive damage in the 11 p.m. attack, but nobody was hurt, the representative Dhondup Gyalpo told RFA.
